springs.title: John Muir founds the Sierra Club
springs.line: Naturalist John Muir’s writings rallied Americans to save wild places; he co-founded the Sierra Club and inspired the national parks movement.

springs.title: Wangari Maathai’s Green Belt Movement
springs.line: Kenyan scientist Wangari Maathai got rural women planting trees, growing a movement that planted tens of millions and earned her a Nobel.

springs.title: Al Gore’s An Inconvenient Truth
springs.line: Al Gore’s climate slideshow became a hit film that alarmed millions about global warming; he shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

protests.title: The Revolutions of 1848
protests.line: Revolutions spread from Paris to Vienna, Berlin, Milan and Budapest within weeks, as crowds demanded constitutions, voting rights and national freedom.

protests.title: The revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe
protests.line: Protests and strikes swept Eastern Europe, toppling communist governments from Poland to Romania within months and bringing down the Berlin Wall.

protests.title: The global Iraq war protests
protests.line: On one day, millions marched against the coming Iraq war in about 600 cities, from Rome and London to Sydney.

protests.title: The Arab Spring and Occupy protests
protests.line: Uprisings spread from Tunisia across the Arab world, and Occupy protest camps soon appeared in hundreds of cities worldwide.

oil.title: The US oil embargo on Japan
oil.line: The US halted oil exports to Japan, which imported most of its oil from America, pushing Tokyo toward war.

oil.title: The Suez Crisis
oil.line: During the Suez war, Egypt blocked the canal and Saudi Arabia embargoed Britain and France, bringing petrol rationing to Britain.

oil.title: The 2009 Russia-Ukraine gas cutoff
oil.line: Russia cut gas to Ukraine in a price dispute, and transit stopped for two weeks, leaving parts of Europe cold in midwinter.

saigon.title: The British retreat from Kabul
saigon.line: About 4,500 British and Indian troops and 12,000 civilians left Kabul in winter under a truce; almost all were killed or captured.

saigon.title: Britain’s rushed exit from India
saigon.line: Britain moved India’s independence up by ten months; partition into India and Pakistan uprooted over 10 million people amid mass killings.

saigon.title: France’s exit from Algeria
saigon.line: After an eight-year war, France left Algeria; some 800,000 settlers fled within months, and many Algerians who served France were killed.

volcker.title: The Fed’s post-war rate hikes
volcker.line: To stop post-World War I inflation, the Fed raised its discount rate to 7%; prices fell sharply and a severe recession followed.

volcker.title: Turkey’s steep rate hikes
volcker.line: After cutting rates as inflation soared past 80%, Turkey’s central bank raised them from 8.5% to 50% in under a year.

chernobyl.title: The Three Mile Island accident
chernobyl.line: A Pennsylvania reactor partly melted down; no one died, but public fear soared and many Americans turned against nuclear power.

tiananmen.title: The May Fourth Movement
tiananmen.line: Beijing students protested the Versailles deal giving Shandong to Japan, sparking a movement for democracy and science that 1989 protesters invoked.

tiananmen.title: The 1976 Tiananmen Incident
tiananmen.line: Crowds mourning Premier Zhou Enlai filled Tiananmen Square with wreaths and poems criticizing radical leaders, until police and militia cleared them.

tiananmen.title: Hong Kong’s Umbrella Movement
tiananmen.line: Protesters occupied main Hong Kong streets for 79 days, demanding open elections for the city’s leader and shielding themselves with umbrellas.

tiananmen.title: China’s blank paper protests
tiananmen.line: After a deadly Urumqi fire, crowds in Shanghai, Beijing and other cities protested COVID lockdowns, holding blank paper to signal censored speech.

netscape.title: The first radio broadcasting boom
netscape.line: Pittsburgh’s KDKA began regular commercial broadcasts, setting off a craze that put radio sets in millions of homes within five years.

netscape.title: The launch of the iPhone
netscape.line: Apple’s iPhone put the web, music and phone in one touchscreen device; within a decade, billions of people carried smartphones.

dolly.title: The first genetically engineered bacteria
dolly.line: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer spliced foreign genes into bacteria, prompting scientists to pause such work and meet at Asilomar in 1975.

dolly.title: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby
dolly.line: Louise Brown, the first baby conceived outside the body, was born in England, setting off a global debate over “test-tube babies”.

dolly.title: The first cell with a synthetic genome
dolly.line: Craig Venter’s team made a bacterium run on a lab-built genome, and President Obama asked his bioethics commission to study the risks.

deepblue.title: IBM’s Watson wins Jeopardy!
deepblue.line: IBM’s Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, the quiz show’s biggest champions, by answering clues written in everyday language.

deepblue.title: AI beats top poker pros
deepblue.line: Carnegie Mellon’s Libratus beat four top professionals at no-limit Texas hold’em, a game of bluffing and hidden cards, over 120,000 hands.

y2k.title: The AT&T long-distance network crash
y2k.line: A bug in a software update crashed AT&T’s long-distance network for nine hours, blocking tens of millions of calls across the US.

y2k.title: The WannaCry ransomware attack
y2k.line: WannaCry ransomware locked over 200,000 computers in about 150 countries, forcing British hospitals to cancel thousands of appointments.

y2k.title: The great Facebook outage
y2k.line: A faulty command during routine maintenance knocked Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp offline for about six hours for billions of users.

dotcom.title: Britain’s Railway Mania
dotcom.line: Britons poured savings into hundreds of new railway schemes, many never built; when share prices collapsed, thousands of investors were ruined.

dotcom.title: The Panic of 1873
dotcom.line: After a US railroad boom, Jay Cooke’s bank collapsed under Northern Pacific debts, setting off a panic and a years-long depression.

blackout.title: The Northeast blackout of 1965
blackout.line: A wrongly set relay near Niagara Falls triggered a cascade that left about 30 million people in the Northeast and Ontario dark.

blackout.title: The New York City blackout of 1977
blackout.line: Lightning strikes blacked out New York City for about a day, and looting and arson broke out across many neighborhoods.

blackout.title: India’s 2012 grid collapse
blackout.line: Two grid failures in two days left over 600 million people in northern and eastern India without power, the largest blackout recorded.
